blocks.text: The Ministry of Works used computers for engineering decisions involving terrain, cost and competing designs. A. C. Shailes’s 1980 account traces its Computer Services Section to 1966 and describes the Vogel Computer Centre as a specialist service for engineering and scientific work.

blocks.text: For the Clutha Valley development, engineers examined ten alternatives for relocating the highway between Cromwell and Clyde. Shailes reported that reduced earthworks on the selected route were estimated to save $1.5 million against the best of the first three alternatives, at the contract rates then in use. The machine widened the comparison; engineers set the constraints and assessed the design.

blocks.text: The Mangaweka road–rail deviation gives a more vivid example. A press statement from the early 1970s, reproduced in Shailes’s account, says Ministry engineers used aerial photographs and programmed gradients and other controls to generate route lines with lower earthworks. The estimates were specific to the proposal and the prices of the day, but the method shows computers being used to search a real terrain problem rather than merely print coordinates.

blocks.text: A 1969 account described a contouring programme for grid surveys; G. J. Harrington’s 1976 work used irregularly spaced stadia readings to build contours. That output sits on the edge of the next shift: calculation was starting to produce reusable digital map geometry.
